a: A word came to Jeremiah from the LORD.
p: Chapter 26 dates a Temple speech to the start of Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 BC. Many link it to this one.
b: Jeremiah 26:1–6 gives the same message as 7:1–15 with a date: "the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim" (26:1), the year after Josiah died at Megiddo (609 BC). Many scholars read chapter 7 as the sermon and chapter 26 as the story of what it cost him. Others think chapter 7 is a longer or earlier speech, perhaps from Josiah's time, because it calls the Temple's security a lie and Josiah's reform had just cleaned the Temple. Critical scholars also ask how much of the prose is Jeremiah's own wording and how much was shaped later in the style of Deuteronomy (the "Deuteronomistic" editors). The Greek lacks 7:1 and the first half of 7:2, so the setting at the gate is a plus of the longer Hebrew edition.

a: Then I will let you stay in this place.
t: Let you stay, or live with you?
p: The same Hebrew letters can mean "I will let you live here" or "I will live with you here."
b: The Hebrew word ashkenah is pointed in the Masoretic Text as a causative: "I will cause you to dwell." The Greek reads it the same way (katoikio, "I will make you live"). But the same consonants can be read "I will dwell with you," and then the promise is that the LORD himself will keep his house among them. Either way the promise is conditional on 7:5–6, and it is the Temple's very presence that the people think guarantees it (7:4). The verb is the root of the Hebrew word for the Presence, shekhinah, in later Jewish writing.

a: The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple: that is what these buildings are!
p: The people chanted that Zion could not fall. Jeremiah calls the chant a lie.
b: Jerusalem's songs said God lived in Zion and would defend it (Psalm 46:4–5; Psalm 48:3). Isaiah's Jerusalem had seen that tested: in 701 BC the Assyrian army left without taking the city (2 Kings 19:34). The slogan grew from that rescue: no harm can come where the LORD's house stands. The threefold repetition sounds like a chant. The Hebrew ends with a plural hemmah, "they," so it points at the whole group of buildings. Jeremiah does not deny that the LORD's house is holy. He says the building cannot protect people who steal, kill and worship Baal (7:9). Even Lamentations 4:12 later remembers how unthinkable the fall had seemed.

a: the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow
p: Foreigner, orphan and widow stand for people with no family to defend them.
b: These three are the people the Torah names again and again as the ones the community must not wrong (Exodus 22:21–22; Deuteronomy 24:17–22; Deuteronomy 27:19). Prophets use the list as a test of a nation's justice (Jeremiah 22:3; Zechariah 7:10; Malachi 3:5). Jeremiah puts it before the Temple gate because the people are going in to worship while the law's demands are broken outside. See also the commands on murder, stealing and adultery in 7:9.

a: send up smoke to Baal
p: Baal was the storm god of Canaan. His worship kept returning to Judah.
b: "Baal" means "lord." He was the Canaanite storm and fertility god, and there were many local Baals (the Hebrew in 9:14 is plural). Kings and prophets show his cult in Judah under Manasseh, and Josiah removed the vessels made for Baal from the Temple (2 Kings 21:3; 2 Kings 23:4–5). Jeremiah's lists of sins here follow the Ten Commandments, then add Baal and "gods you have never known." The Hebrew has the order steal, murder, adultery, while the Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has the order of the Ten Commandments: murder, adultery, steal (Exodus 20:13–15).

a: We are rescued!
p: The people say they are "rescued." The sentence can mean they are safe to keep sinning.
b: The Hebrew verb nitsalnu means "we have been delivered." Jeremiah's hearers say it after they have come to the Temple, as if worship cleared them. The next words, lema'an, usually mean "in order to," and the Plain keeps that sting: they say it "so you can go on" doing the abhorrent things. Some commentators soften it to "with the result that," but the sharper sense is possible: the Temple has become their permission slip. Compare 7:4, where "the LORD's temple" is the slogan. The Greek has the worshipers say something different ("We have kept away from these abominations"); see the variant.

a: a cave for bandits
p: Jesus joined Jeremiah's words to Isaiah's when he drove the traders out.
b: Matthew 21:13, Mark 11:17 and Luke 19:46 all have Jesus say the Temple has become "a cave for bandits" (the wording of the Plain in those Gospels), after Isaiah 56:7, "my house will be called a house of prayer." The Greek words in the Gospels, spelaion leston, are the words of the Greek Jeremiah in this verse, and the Plain uses the same English in both places. A cave is a hideout, and many readers take Jeremiah's charge to be that people sin outside and run to God's house for cover (7:9–10). Whether Jesus meant the traders' profits, the Temple's corruption, or Jeremiah's larger warning that the building would fall (Mark 13:2) is discussed under the New Testament passages.
orig: מְעָרַת פָּרִצִים (me'arat paritsim), 'a cave of violent men'

a: my place that was in Shiloh
p: Shiloh once held the tent and the ark. Jeremiah says it was destroyed. Excavations show a burned layer.
b: Shiloh, about 20 miles north of Jerusalem, was Israel's sanctuary in the days of Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 1–4). Psalm 78:60 says that God "left the tabernacle of Shiloh behind." The Bible never tells how it ended; Jeremiah 7:14 and 26:6 assume the audience knows. Excavators found a destroyed city from about 1050 BC (the Danish dig and Israel Finkelstein's later work), which fits, but who burned it and exactly when are debated. Jeremiah's argument is plain: if the LORD let his own sanctuary fall because of his people's evil, Jerusalem is not exempt.

a: the whole offspring of Ephraim
p: Ephraim is the northern kingdom. Assyria had deported it a century earlier.
b: "Ephraim" stands for the northern kingdom of Israel, whose capital Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6–18). Jeremiah calls its people "your kin," the same family of tribes. His warning to Judah is that the northern exile is the pattern: what happened to Shiloh and then to Ephraim can happen to Jerusalem.

a: do not pray on behalf of this people
p: The LORD tells Jeremiah to stop praying for the people. It comes again in 11:14, 14:11 and 15:1.
b: A prophet was expected to plead for the people (Moses, Exodus 32:11–14; Samuel, 1 Samuel 12:23; Amos, Amos 7:2–6). Here the LORD forbids it, and repeats the ban in 11:14 and 14:11. The reason is not that prayer is wrong. The verdict has been given, as 7:12–15 shows, and the people keep sinning. Jeremiah 15:1 says that even Moses and Samuel could not turn the LORD back now. The ban shows how far the crisis has gone, and it makes Jeremiah's later pleas (14:7–9, 19–22) harder for him. The prophet is told not to pray; the text does not say God has stopped being merciful (compare 12:15).
r: Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23; Amos 7:2–6; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1

a: Do not press me
p: In 2 Maccabees, Jeremiah appears in a vision still praying for the people. Churches read that differently.
b: The Second Book of Maccabees (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, not for Protestants or Jews) tells how Judas Maccabeus saw a vision of the dead high priest Onias and of a man of splendor, and Onias says: "This is the lover of his brothers, the one who prays much for the people and the holy city, Jeremiah the prophet of God" (2 Maccabees 15:14). So a writer of the second century BC pictured Jeremiah praying even after the ban of this verse and after his death. Catholic and Orthodox teaching cites such passages for the intercession of the saints. See the card on this chapter.

a: the Queen of Heaven
t: Who was the Queen of Heaven?
p: She is usually identified with Ishtar or Astarte. No inscription found in Judah calls anyone by this title.
b: Malkat hashamayim appears only here and in 44:17–25. Akkadian texts call the goddess Ishtar "queen of heaven," and Ishtar and the West Semitic Astarte were goddesses of love, war and the planet Venus. That is the usual identification (Weinfeld, Ackerman, Day). Some argue for Asherah or Anat, or for a Judean blend of several goddesses. The evidence from the land itself is indirect. At Kuntillet 'Ajrud, a site in the northeast Sinai on the Judah–Sinai border (about 800 BC), inscriptions bless people "by Yahweh of Samaria" and "by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah"; whether "asherah" means a goddess or a cult object is disputed, and the site is not in Judah itself. Small female figurines also turn up in Judean homes. But nothing found in Judah names the Queen of Heaven. In 44:15–19 the women say they did this before Josiah's reform and prospered. For the Egyptian evidence, see the note on "to make me angry."

a: to make cakes
p: The Hebrew for "cakes" is a rare word. Akkadian has a matching word for cakes baked for Ishtar.
b: Kawwanim occurs only here and in 44:19. It matches the Akkadian kamanu, the name of a cake offered to Ishtar in Mesopotamian texts. The Judean women of 44:19 say they baked such cakes "in her image" (the Hebrew is debated), and the Greek (Codex Vaticanus) does not translate the word: it writes it in Greek letters (chauonas) and reads "the army of heaven" for "the Queen of Heaven" (see the variant). The scene is a family act: children, fathers, women. It is home religion, not state religion. That is why Jeremiah 44 has the women answering for themselves.

a: pour out drink offerings
p: Wine or water poured out on the ground for a god. The LORD's own law has a drink offering too.
b: A drink offering (nesek) was a liquid poured out before a god. The LORD's law had its own (Numbers 15:5–10), so the offense is the recipient, not the act: "to other gods." The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) writes that they "poured out drinks to strange gods." 4QJer-a preserves the end of this verse ("to other gods, to make me angry") with the Masoretic wording where the scroll is not broken.

a: to make me angry
t: The Queen of Heaven in Egypt
p: Aramaic letters from Egypt greet a temple of the Queen of Heaven, and Elephantine had Anat-Yahu. How far does that reach?
b: Jeremiah 44:1 puts Judean refugees in Pathros, which is Upper Egypt, and 44:15–19 has them keep up the cult there. The Aramaic evidence from the same region is later than Jeremiah, by roughly a century or more. Letters found at Hermopolis (late sixth or early fifth century BC) send greetings to temples at Syene (modern Aswan), among them a temple of Bethel and a temple of the Queen of Heaven (Porten and Yardeni, as reported by Mondriaan). Nearby Elephantine had a Jewish military colony whose papyri include an oath "by AnatYHW" and mention Anat-Bethel (Porten; Mondriaan). Karel van der Toorn argues that Anat-Yahu was an Aramaean creation modeled on Anat-Bethel, not a Judean survival from Jeremiah's day, and Mondriaan notes there is no evidence that Anat was worshiped in Israel. So the title is attested in Aramaic in Upper Egypt in the fifth century BC, but the evidence does not show who she was, and it does not show a Judean cult of her in 600 BC. See 44.

a: It will burn and will not go out.
t: A fire that is not put out
p: The fire of the LORD's anger is described like the fire in other prophets and in the Gospels.
b: The same words describe the burning anger of God in Jeremiah 4:4 and 17:27 and in Isaiah 1:31; Isaiah 66:24 speaks of a fire that "will not be put out." Jesus uses Isaiah 66:24's words about Gehenna (Mark 9:48). The ordinary sense in Jeremiah is a fire that burns the land until nothing is left, not an account of the afterlife.

a: Eat the meat yourselves!
t: Add them up and eat it all
p: A burnt offering was burned whole. Telling them to eat it too says: to me it is only meat.
b: A burnt offering (olah) was entirely burned on the altar; the worshipper ate none of it (Leviticus 1). A shared sacrifice (zevach) was partly eaten. The LORD tells them to pile one on the other and eat the whole thing, which is a bitter joke: the offerings without obedience are only a meal.

a: I did not speak to your ancestors
p: Leviticus is full of sacrifice law. How can the LORD say he gave no orders about it?
b: Four readings. (1) A Hebrew way of saying "not so much": obedience first, offerings second (compare 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6). (2) The words refer to the day of the exodus: at that point the people were given the covenant call to obey (Exodus 19:4–6), not yet the sacrifice laws of Sinai. Rashi reads it so, saying the condition began at Exodus 19:5. (3) Radak, the medieval Jewish commentator, argues that the Ten Commandments never mention sacrifice, and that individual offerings were an option the law allowed, while the daily offering served the community. (4) Critical scholars often hear a prophetic protest against the cult, or a view that the priestly sacrifice laws of Leviticus were not yet in force or known in Jeremiah's circle. The Greek (Vaticanus) has the same denial.
r: Leviticus 1–7; Exodus 19:4–6; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–25; Psalm 51:16–17; Isaiah 1:11–17

a: I will be your God, and you will be my people
p: This line summarizes the covenant. It returns in Jeremiah 11:4, 24:7, 30:22 and 31:33.
b: "I will be your God and you will be my people" is the shortest statement of the covenant (Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12). Jeremiah quotes it back to the people here, uses it again in 11:4, and promises it in the new covenant (31:33). Paul applies it to the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation 21:3 sees it fulfilled at the end.
r: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 11:4; Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3

a: the stubbornness of their evil hearts
p: Jeremiah's favorite phrase for the people's will: a heart that has set itself hard.
b: Shrirut lev, "stubbornness of heart," is almost Jeremiah's own phrase: it occurs here, in 9:14 and 11:8, and in 3:17; 13:10; 16:12; 18:12; 23:17, and nowhere else outside Deuteronomy 29:19 and Psalm 81:12. The "heart" in Hebrew is the center of thought and will, so this is a stubborn mind. The Greek has "the thoughts of their evil heart."

a: my servants the prophets
p: Jeremiah and the Kings writers see the prophets as a long line of sent messengers.
b: "My servants the prophets" is a standard phrase in the history in Kings and in Jeremiah (2 Kings 17:13; Jeremiah 25:4; 26:5; 29:19; 35:15; 44:4). It makes each prophet the next in a line begun at the exodus. Critical scholars connect the phrase to the Deuteronomistic editors; traditional readers take it as Jeremiah's own way of speaking. Either way it frames his own work as one more sending, which will also be refused.

a: Faithfulness is gone.
p: Hebrew emunah can be "faithfulness" or "truth." Both ideas fit.
b: Emunah comes from the root of "amen" and means what can be relied on: faithfulness, firmness, truth. Jeremiah 5:1 asks if one person in Jerusalem practices it, and 9:3 says the people are not strong in the land "for faithfulness." The Greek has pistis, the word later used for Christian "faith."

a: Shave off your long hair
t: A cut that is grief, not vow
p: The Hebrew means the hair of a dedicated person, cut off in mourning. The command is to a woman.
b: Nezer is the "consecration," the long hair of a Nazirite (Numbers 6:7) that was cut at the end of a vow. Here it is the hair of a person dedicated to the LORD. Cutting it and throwing it away is the sign of grief (Job 1:20; Micah 1:16; Isaiah 15:2). The verbs are feminine singular, so the speaker addresses a woman, probably Daughter Zion, Jerusalem personified. The poem goes on to a funeral song on the bare hills, where pagan shrines had stood.

a: the high places of Topheth
t: Topheth and the Valley of Ben-hinnom
p: Topheth was a shrine in the valley south of Jerusalem where children were burned. Its name is debated.
b: The valley of Ben-hinnom runs along Jerusalem's southwest side. Topheth was a shrine there where people burned their sons and daughters in the fire. Ahaz and Manasseh did it (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and Josiah made the place unclean so that no one could again (2 Kings 23:10). The name's meaning is debated: a fire pit, or the Hebrew bosheth, "shame," re-pointed. Whether this was Molech worship or a different rite, and whether the children were killed or only dedicated, is discussed in the topic on Molech (Day; Heider). Carthage had a similar "tophet," a cemetery with urns of burned infants; scholars still argue whether those were sacrifices (Stager and Wolff) or children who died young. Jeremiah calls it something the LORD never commanded (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2–5).
r: 2 Kings 23:10; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 19:5; Jeremiah 32:35

a: I never commanded it. It never came up into my heart.
t: Three things that never crossed his mind
p: Jeremiah 19:5 has a third clause. The Talmud finds three child sacrifices in it.
b: Jeremiah 19:5 adds a middle clause, "nor did I speak of it," between the two found here. The Babylonian Talmud (Taanit 4a) matches the three clauses to the sacrifice of Mesha's son (2 Kings 3:27), of Jephthah's daughter (Judges 11), and of Isaac (Genesis 22), as three cases the LORD never asked for. This is one Jewish reading; the verse here has only the first and third clauses.

a: the Valley of Slaughter
t: Was Gehenna a burning garbage dump?
p: Popular books say Gehenna was Jerusalem's trash fire. The evidence for this is late.
b: Jeremiah renames the valley "Valley of Slaughter" because of the corpses it will hold. It later became Gehenna, the Greek form of Ge Hinnom, the New Testament's word for the place of punishment (Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43–48). The claim that Jews of Jesus' day used the valley as a burning dump comes no earlier than the medieval commentator Radak (on Psalm 27:13), as Lloyd Bailey reports, and has no support in sources from Jesus' time. The Bible gives the valley a different record: child sacrifice (7:31) and judgment (19:6–9).

a: No one will be there to frighten them away.
p: Left unburied, eaten by birds. It is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26.
b: Deuteronomy 28:26 lists this among the curses of the covenant: corpses left as food for the birds and animals, with no one to scare them off. Jeremiah repeats it as fact (16:4; 19:7; 34:20). Proper burial was a sacred duty, and its denial the sharpest shame (8:1–2).

a: the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
p: Joy at weddings ends. The same pair of voices returns in 16:9 and 25:10, and is promised back in 33:11.
b: The voices of a groom and a bride stand for an ordinary, happy village. Jeremiah says they will stop (16:9; 25:10) and later says they will be heard again (33:10–11). Revelation 18:23 borrows the line for the fall of Babylon. The Plain uses the same English each time: "the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride" (7:34; 16:9; 25:10; 33:11).

a: they will bring out of their graves the bones of the kings of Judah
p: To drag the dead out of their graves was a final shame. Josiah had done it to others.
b: Josiah had burned the bones of priests from the graves at Bethel (2 Kings 23:16). Now the same shame will come to Judah's kings, officials, priests, prophets and ordinary citizens. In the ancient world rest in the family tomb was the hope of every person, and exposure was a curse (Jeremiah 22:19). The Greek (Vaticanus) has the same list. The ones named are the very leaders who led the people to worship the sky (8:2).

a: the ones they loved and served, the ones they followed, asked for guidance and bowed down to
p: The five verbs of devotion once belonged to the LORD alone.
b: Love, serve, walk after, seek and bow down are the verbs Deuteronomy uses for loyalty to the LORD (Deuteronomy 6:5, 13; 10:12; 13:4). Jeremiah gives them to the sun, the moon and the stars, which were worshiped in Judah under Assyrian and Babylonian influence (2 Kings 21:3, 5; 23:5; Jeremiah 19:13). The punishment fits: the bones lie under the sky they worshiped.

a: Death will be chosen over life
p: Moses told Israel to choose life. Jeremiah says the survivors will choose death.
b: Deuteronomy 30:19 ends with the command "choose life." Jeremiah 8:3 says that when the survivors are scattered, they will choose death. The poet means that the life they will have in exile will be worse than death (compare Jonah 4:3; Revelation 9:6).

a: Does anyone turn away and never turn back?
p: The same Hebrew verb shuv means to turn back to God and to turn away from him. Jeremiah plays on it.
b: Shuv means "turn" or "return." In 8:4–6 it appears about six times, in the forms "turns away," "turns back," "a turning away that never ends" (meshuvah nitsachat), "refuse to turn back," and "keeps turning back to his own course." The pun is on the question: a person who falls gets up; one who turns away should turn back. Judah has done neither. The prophet's call to repent (3:12–14, 22; 4:1) uses the same word. The Plain keeps "turn" throughout so that English readers can follow it.

a: The stork too, up in the sky, knows the times set for it.
p: The Hebrew name of the stork means "the loyal one."
b: Bird migration over Judah is vast, and the prophet notes that the birds keep their calendar. The Hebrew name for the stork, chasidah, comes from the root of chesed (loyal love): the bird has the name of the quality Israel lacks. The four birds named here are the stork, the turtledove, the swift or swallow, and the crane (the last is uncertain); identifying them is not sure.

a: the LORD's order
p: Mishpat usually means justice. Here it is the ordered way the LORD set for his people.
b: Mishpat is the "right order" of things, a ruling, or justice. The Greek has "the judgments of the LORD." The point is that birds follow the order God made for them while the people ignore the order he made for them, as in 5:4–5.

a: the LORD's law
p: Torah means "teaching" and, in the written form, "law." Here it is the written law the scribes handle.
b: Torah is "teaching," a parent's or prophet's instruction, and it also names the written law. Here, because scribes are handling it with a pen, the Plain says "law." In 9:13 the LORD says they have left "my law, the one I set out in front of them." Jeremiah's own use of the word is mixed: he speaks of the priests' torah being lost (2:8, 18:18) and, in 31:33, of the torah written on the heart.

a: the scribes' lying pen has turned it into a lie
t: The lying pen of the scribes
p: The Hebrew is short and can be read three ways. All are about what scribes do to the law.
b: The Hebrew says, roughly, "into a lie it [or he] made it, the lying pen of the scribes." Readings: (1) the scribes copy or teach the law falsely; (2) the scribes write official documents, such as legal rulings and decrees, that deceive; (3) some modern scholars think the target is the law-book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22:8), others reject this. The word for "pen" is et, the writing stylus or reed. The Greek has "a lying reed to the scribes was made in vain," with a different sense. Jeremiah's quarrel is with those who claim authority from the written law while ignoring its demands.

a: "Peace, peace,"
p: These lines repeat 6:13–15 with four small differences. The same false comfort is the target.
b: Verses 8:10b–12 repeat 6:12–15, and the Plain gives the shared lines the same English in both places. The Hebrew differs in four places, and the Plain keeps each difference (the Plain has "abomination" in both, as 6:15 does): (1) 8:10 has "their wives to others, their fields to those who take them over"; 6:12 has "their houses will pass to others, their fields and their wives together." (2) 8:10 has "from small to great"; 6:13 has "from their small to their great." (3) 8:11 has "my dear people" (bat 'ammi, literally "the daughter of my people"); 6:14 has "my people" ('ammi). (4) 8:12 has "at the time of their punishment"; 6:15 has "at the time I have visited them." The false prophets' slogan "Peace, peace" is also the target of Ezekiel 13:10 and has an echo in Paul's "when they say 'Peace and security'" (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) lacks 8:10b–12 here; see the variants.

a: What I gave them will pass away from them.
t: A verse that cannot be read with confidence
p: The Hebrew is hard. The Greek reads the whole verse differently.
b: The Hebrew opens with a harvest word twice (asoph asifem, "gathering I will gather them" or "I will end them") and closes with the puzzling "I gave them, they will pass over them." Readings of the last clause: what I gave will pass away from them; I appointed ones who will overrun them; or an invading force crosses over them. The Greek has a different verse: "they will gather their produce," with no mention of an ending. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and keeps the first reading.

a: be silenced
p: The Hebrew uses one verb for being silent and for being destroyed.
b: Damam means "be still" and, by extension, "be destroyed." The Hebrew plays on it: "let us be silenced there, for the LORD has silenced us." The Plain keeps the pun, and the gloss gives the second sense, being put to an end. The Greek says the LORD "has cast us off."

a: poisoned water
p: The Hebrew rosh may be a bitter, poisonous plant. It pairs with wormwood in Deuteronomy 29:18.
b: Rosh is a poisonous plant (hemlock or similar), also called "gall." Water with it in it is bitter, and fatal in quantity. Deuteronomy 29:18 pairs it with wormwood as the fruit of a root that turns from the LORD; Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15 give the people both. The Plain calls it "poisoned water" here and in 9:15.

a: From Dan
p: Dan was the northernmost town of Israel. The invader comes from there.
b: Dan lay at the northern frontier, so the sound of horses "from Dan" is the sound of an army from the north, as in 4:15 and 6:22. Whether the northern foe is the Scythians, as an older view held, or Babylon is discussed at 4:6 and 6:22.

a: vipers that no charm can tame
p: Charming snakes with a spell was an ancient craft. Here the snakes are beyond it.
b: Psalm 58:4–5 compares the wicked to a deaf viper that ignores the snake charmer, and Ecclesiastes 10:11 mentions a snake that bites before it is charmed. Jeremiah's snakes cannot be charmed at all: no spell will protect the people from them. Numbers 21:6 has the older story of snakes sent on Israel.

a: My cheer is gone, and sorrow rests on me.
t: A verse with one unknown word
p: The first Hebrew word occurs nowhere else. Translations guess.
b: The word mavligiti is found only here. It may come from balag, "to be cheerful," so "my cheer is gone" or "my cheerfulness against sorrow." The KJV reads "when I would comfort myself against sorrow," the BSB "my sorrow is beyond healing," and the YLT "my refreshing for me is sorrow." The Greek attaches the line to 8:17: "bites that cannot be healed, with pain, your heart at a loss." The Plain takes the plainest reading.

a: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her king not in her?"
p: The verse switches speakers three times: the poet, the people, then the LORD.
b: First the poet hears the cry of his people "from a land far away." Then come the people's own words: surely the LORD is in Zion. Then the LORD answers: why did they make me angry with carved images and empty foreign gods? The sequence can be a vision of exiles crying out from far away, or the voice of people in danger of invasion. In either case the people expect God to defend his house (compare 7:4), and the LORD answers with their idol worship. The Hebrew has no word for the change of speaker; the Plain adds "The LORD answers" so that the reader can follow it.

a: Is there no balm in Gilead?
p: Gilead east of the Jordan was famous for a healing resin. Jeremiah asks why no cure comes.
b: Tsori was a resin traded from Gilead (Genesis 37:25; Ezekiel 27:17). It was used for wounds. The question expects the answer "of course there is," and then asks why no cure came up. In the African American spiritual "There Is a Balm in Gilead" the answer is yes: Christ is the balm. In Jeremiah the question is the sorrow itself: there is a healer, and the people will not be healed (compare 46:11).

a: Who will give water to my head
p: English 9:1 is 8:23 in the Hebrew Bible. Every verse in this chapter is one number off.
b: The Hebrew Bible and the Jewish translations end chapter 8 with the verse that English calls 9:1. So English 9:1–26 is Hebrew 8:23–9:25. This site uses the English numbers. The Greek follows the English division. Commentaries on the Hebrew will cite everything in this chapter one lower.

a: so that I could weep day and night
p: Jeremiah is known as the prophet who wept. But it is not clear that it is only his voice.
b: From the Talmud on, tradition made Jeremiah the weeping prophet, and the same tradition made him the author of Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a). Modern scholars hear several voices in these chapters: Jeremiah, the people, Daughter Zion, and the LORD himself, who weeps over his people (12:7–13). Abraham Heschel read the prophet's grief as sharing the divine pathos.

a: a lodge for travelers
p: Jeremiah wishes he could leave his people for the desert. Psalm 55 has the same wish.
b: A melon orechim was a rough caravan stop. Jeremiah's wish to run away from the people he loves, because they are all unfaithful, is like the psalmist's in Psalm 55:6–8. It contrasts with 8:21, where he suffers with them, and shows the pull he feels between the two.

a: every brother is a trickster
p: The Hebrew says "every brother is a Jacob."
b: The Hebrew has aqov ya'aqov, literally "a brother tricks, he tricks," which sounds like the name Yaakov, Jacob, the "heel-grabber" who tricked his brother Esau (Genesis 25:26; 27:35–36). Hosea 12:3 makes the same wordplay. The Greek (Vaticanus) has "every brother will trip up with the heel," keeping the sense.

a: smelt them and test them
p: God as a metal-worker who burns away the dross. See 6:27–30.
b: In 6:27–30 Jeremiah was made an assayer of the people, and the refining failed: the dross would not come out. Here the LORD himself says he must smelt them. The picture of refining with fire returns for the faithful in Malachi 3:2–3 and Zechariah 13:9.

a: hammered arrow
p: A written and a read form differ. One means "hammered," the other "slaughtering."
b: The Masoretes wrote shochet, "slaughtering" or "killing," and marked it to be read shachut, "hammered" (as of hammered gold in 1 Kings 10:16). The Plain follows the read form (the Qere). See the variant for the readings and witnesses.

a: Will I not punish them for these things, the LORD declares?
p: These two lines are word for word the refrain of 5:9 and 5:29.
b: The same two questions appear in 5:9 and 5:29 (see there). The refrain closes each of the first sections of the book's indictment, here as the answer to the lies of 9:3–8.

a: wormwood
p: A bitter plant. It stands for bitterness and poison in the Bible.
b: La'anah is wormwood or a similar bitter herb. Deuteronomy 29:18 warns of a root that bears poison and wormwood; Lamentations 3:15, 19 says God filled the speaker with wormwood. Revelation 8:11 names a star "Wormwood." The Greek has "I will feed them pains" here.

a: the women who wail
p: Hired women led the weeping at funerals. Jeremiah tells them to start now.
b: Mourning women (mequnenot) were skilled in laments (2 Chronicles 35:25; Amos 5:16; Matthew 9:23). Jeremiah calls for them to come early, because the whole city is about to die. The call to teach their daughters a funeral song (9:20) is a call to pass on a tradition for a time when everyone has a loss.

a: Death has crept up to our windows
p: Death is pictured as a person who climbs into a house. A Canaanite myth has a similar scene.
b: Death comes in through the windows of the palace. In the Canaanite Baal Cycle from Ugarit, the god Baal at first refuses to put a window in his house, for fear that Death (Mot) would come in. Commentators have compared the two since the mid-1900s. The link is suggestive but unproven: the Hebrew simply gives Death a body, and Jeremiah may be adapting a common picture.

a: A wise person should not boast about his wisdom.
t: The only thing to boast of
p: Paul compresses these two verses to "let the one who boasts boast in the Lord."
b: Paul's short form "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17) condenses these verses. In 1 Corinthians he uses it against Corinthians who boast of wisdom. The Jeremiah passage sets three goods people prize (wisdom, strength, riches) against a fourth: knowing the LORD and the three things he loves.

a: loyal love, justice and righteousness
p: Three words for the LORD's character, and for what he wants from people.
b: Chesed (loyal love), mishpat (justice) and tsedaqah (righteousness) are the LORD's three ways of acting on the earth, and Jeremiah says that Josiah's justice and righteousness for the poor was what it meant to "know" the LORD (22:15–16). Knowing the LORD in this verse means practicing them, not only knowing about him.

a: everyone circumcised in a foreskin
p: The Hebrew is a riddle: circumcised "in" a foreskin. Readers take it in two ways.
b: Mul be'orlah is literally "circumcised in foreskin." Reading 1: those circumcised in the body but with the foreskin of the heart, as in 9:26 (the WEB has "circumcised only in their flesh"; the ASV "circumcised in their uncircumcision"). Reading 2: "the circumcised along with the uncircumcised," that is, everyone, whether or not circumcised in the body (the KJV has "circumcised with the uncircumcised"; the BSB "circumcised yet uncircumcised"). Rashi, on the verse the Hebrew numbers 9:25 (English 9:26), says of the nations in the list: "These were the neighbors of Eretz Israel, and they were punished shortly after her." The Greek reads "all those circumcised in their foreskin," and its list at 9:26 names Egypt, Idumaea, Edom, Ammon and Moab, and does not name Judah. The same idea of a circumcised heart is in 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16; Romans 2:25–29.

a: hair cut at the corners
t: The clipped hair of desert tribes
p: Some desert Arabs cut their hair around the temples. Leviticus forbids the style to Israelites.
b: Qetsutsei pe'ah, "those cut at the edge," are people who trim the hair at the temples. Leviticus 19:27 forbids Israelites to do it. Herodotus (Histories 3.8) says the Arabs shaved their hair in a circle. Jeremiah lists them with Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab (compare 25:23; 49:32) to say that all these nations circumcise but are untouched in the heart, and Israel is no better.

a: the signs in the sky
p: Babylonian priests read eclipses and comets as messages. Jeremiah says not to fear them.
b: Babylonian scholars kept long records of eclipses, comets and planet movements and used them to advise the king. Isaiah 47:13 mocks the same practice. Deuteronomy 18:9–14 bans it for Israel. Jeremiah's hearers were about to come under Babylon's power, and the pressure to take the stars seriously was real.

a: empty breath
p: Jeremiah's word for idols is hevel, the same word as in Ecclesiastes.
b: Hevel is a puff of breath. Ecclesiastes uses it for the shortness of life. Jeremiah uses it for idols (2:5; 8:19; 10:3, 8, 15; 14:22; 16:19): they are as insubstantial as breath. The Plain says "empty breath" here, not "vanity."

a: Someone cuts a tree from the forest.
p: Isaiah and the Psalms mock idols the same way. A later Jewish letter expands this chapter.
b: Isaiah 44:9–20 and 40:19–20 and Psalm 115:4–8 and 135:15–18 mock idols as man-made things that cannot speak, walk or breathe. The Letter of Jeremiah (an Apocrypha work, Baruch 6 in Catholic Bibles) develops this chapter at length, and its refrain is "they are no gods." Both are satire, not a description of how idol-worshipers understood their statues: ancient worshipers held that a god was present in the image once it was consecrated.
r: Isaiah 40:19–20; Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8; Psalm 135:15–18; Letter of Jeremiah 6–7

a: a scarecrow in a cucumber field
p: The Hebrew can mean a scarecrow in a cucumber field or a palm-like pillar of beaten work.
b: Tomer miqshah is read two ways. (1) A "scarecrow in a cucumber field" (miqshah as a cucumber patch, as in Isaiah 1:8). The Letter of Jeremiah 70 (Baruch 6:70) has the scarecrow in a cucumber bed. (2) A "palm of turned work" or hammered column, which is how the KJV, ASV, WEB and YLT take it. The Greek (Vaticanus) has "they are hammered silver," which fits the second. The Plain takes the first. Both make the same point: the idol is lifeless, standing where it was put.

a: You are great, and great is your name in strength.
t: A short text and a long text
p: The Greek and one Qumran scroll leave out 10:6–8 and 10:10. This is the best test case for the two editions of Jeremiah.
b: Verses 10:6–8 and 10:10 praise the LORD and mock the idols. The Greek lacks them, and so does 4QJer-b (4Q71), a Qumran copy of the second century BC (published estimates run from about 200 BC to the middle of the century). The transcription preserves 4QJer-b from 9:23 to 10:21, and in it 10:1–5, 9 and 11–21 are present without 6–8 and 10. 4QJer-a (4Q70) has 10:10 as the Masoretic Text has it. Emanuel Tov uses this as one of his main examples that the Greek translates an earlier, shorter edition of Jeremiah, and that the longer Hebrew edition grew by additions. A minority view holds that the Greek translator abridged. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, the edition the Jewish and most Christian Bibles use, and shows the omissions as variants.

a: This is what you are to say to them
p: The only verse of Jeremiah written in Aramaic. Both Qumran scrolls that have it keep it in Aramaic.
b: Verse 11 is in Aramaic, the everyday language of the Babylonians and the Persian empire, not Hebrew. It is a sentence for the exiles to say to idol-worshipers: the gods who did not make heaven and earth will perish. Rashi (read on Sefaria) takes it as the text of a letter Jeremiah sent to Jeconiah and the exiles in Babylon, to answer the Chaldeans if told to worship idols. The verse has two Aramaic forms of the word "earth": arqa (with a qof) in "the heavens and the earth" and ar'a (with an ayin) in "from the earth." The Leningrad Codex writes both as printed, so this is two spellings of one word, not a wordplay. Both 4QJer-a and 4QJer-b preserve parts of the verse in Aramaic, and both have arqa. The Greek keeps the verse, in Greek, after 10:9, though it lacks 10:10; so does 4QJer-b. The Aramaic verse was therefore part of the shorter edition too.

a: He made the earth with his power.
p: These verses also stand in 51:15–19, and 10:13 is Psalm 135:7.
b: Jeremiah 10:12–16 is repeated almost word for word in 51:15–19, the oracle against Babylon, where it follows the same mockery of idols. Verse 13 is Psalm 135:7 almost exactly, and Psalm 135:15–18 follows with the same idol satire. The common source may be a hymn that both used.

a: Not like these is the one who is Jacob's share
p: The LORD is the portion of his people, as he was for the Levites.
b: "Share" (cheleq) is the land share of each tribe. The Levites had no land, and the LORD was their share (Numbers 18:20). Psalms 16:5; 73:26; 119:57 and Lamentations 3:24 use the same word for the LORD as the share of the individual. In Jeremiah the whole of Jacob has the LORD himself as its share.

a: so that they find out
p: The Hebrew has "so that they may find," with no object.
b: The Hebrew says only "so that they may find." Some add "it" (find out, feel it). The Greek supplies an object: "so that your wound may be found." The Plain keeps the open ending as "find out."

a: My tent is a wreck.
p: The voice mourns a tent, children and a shepherd's help. It sounds like Zion more than Jeremiah.
b: The speaker grieves a ruined tent, snapped cords and lost children. Some hear Jeremiah as the one who feels the nation's loss as his own. Others hear Daughter Zion herself, as in Lamentations 1–2. 4:19–21 is the closest parallel, with the same "tent and curtains." The Greek has "my sons and my sheep are gone," a different second clause.

a: the shepherds
p: In the Bible, "shepherds" often means kings and leaders. See 23:1.
b: Ancient kings were called shepherds. Jeremiah condemns the shepherds of Judah here, in 2:8, in 23:1–4 and 25:34–36. Ezekiel 34 develops it. In 12:10 "many shepherds" may mean the invading Babylonian generals (as in 6:3), or Judah's leaders who ruined it.

a: a great din out of the northern land
t: The foe from the north again
p: Another report of the northern army. The idea comes in 1:14, 4:6 and 6:22.
b: The "land of the north" echoes 1:14; 4:6; 6:22 and 8:16. The poem turns the earlier warning into a rumor already on its way.

a: the way of a human being does not belong to him
p: Proverbs says the same: a person plans, the LORD directs. Jeremiah says it in prayer.
b: Proverbs 16:9 and 20:24 say that a person's steps are the LORD's doing. In Jeremiah's prayer the point is humility: the speaker asks to be corrected, not destroyed (10:24).

a: Correct me, LORD, but by what is just.
p: The LORD later answers this prayer with almost the same words.
b: Jeremiah 30:11 and 46:28 have the LORD promise the nation "I will correct you in justice," the same word and the same phrase. The prayer is answered in the Book of Consolation.

a: Pour out your fury on the nations
p: Psalm 79:6–7 is nearly the same prayer. The Haggadah sings it at Passover.
b: Psalm 79:6–7 repeats this verse with small differences ("kingdoms" for "families," and a shorter second half). Which came first is debated; both are prayers after the fall of Jerusalem. The Passover Haggadah's "Pour out your wrath" draws on Psalm 79:6–7, Psalm 69:25 and Lamentations 3:66. Jeremiah 10:25 is not a call for personal revenge. It is the cry of one whose people have been devoured, put in God's hands (compare 11:20).

a: Hear the words of this covenant
p: The covenant of Sinai, or the covenant Josiah made in 622 BC? Or the book of Deuteronomy?
b: Verses 4–5 trace the covenant to the day of the exodus (Sinai or Horeb). But "the words of this covenant" is also the phrase for the law book found in the Temple under Josiah, which Josiah read aloud and made the people join (2 Kings 23:1–3). Some scholars say Jeremiah preached the reform after 622 (11:6 orders him to cry the words in the cities of Judah). Others think the Deuteronomistic editors wrote the chapter later, and Jeremiah's own words are the poetry at the end (11:15–23). The text itself does not say how the exodus covenant and Josiah's renewal fit, and the book's attitude to Josiah's reform is discussed in the commentaries.

a: the iron furnace
p: Slavery in Egypt is a furnace: it burns, but it also forms a people.
b: Deuteronomy 4:20 and 1 Kings 8:51 call Egypt an "iron furnace," a smelting oven for iron. It is an image of harsh suffering. The same image of a furnace as a place of testing returns in Isaiah 48:10 and Ezekiel 22:18–22.

a: "Amen, LORD."
p: Jeremiah's one-word answer. He says it again, bitterly, to Hananiah in 28:6.
b: Amen means "so be it" or "it is firm." People said it at the end of a curse (Deuteronomy 27:15–26). Jeremiah answers the covenant's curse (11:3) with it. In 28:6 he says "Amen!" to Hananiah's promise of peace and then shows it is false. The Greek has "Let it be so, LORD."

a: A plot has been found
p: The word means a political plot. The covenant was a treaty, and breaking it was treason.
b: Qesher is the word for a plot against a king (2 Kings 12:20; 15:30). The covenant with the LORD had the form of the treaties between a great king and his vassals, and Assyrian treaties from the 600s BC, such as the succession treaty of Esarhaddon, have curses like those in Deuteronomy 28. Jeremiah says Judah has committed treason: not against a throne but against the LORD.

a: the Shame
p: Scribes replaced the name of Baal with "Shame." The same swap appears in people's names.
b: Bosheth means "shame." Hebrew scribes read it in place of "Baal" (Jeremiah 3:24; Hosea 9:10). It also changed names: Saul's son Ishbaal appears as Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:8) and Jonathan's son Meribbaal as Mephibosheth. The altars here stand for Baal.

a: do not pray on behalf of this people
p: The second of three bans on prayer for the people (7:16, 11:14, 14:11). See 7:16.
b: The command repeats 7:16 in the same words. It comes again in 14:11. The Greek (Vaticanus) has the same ban with a shorter ending. The ban means that the LORD will not listen when they cry out in disaster (11:11), which fits what the covenant says in Deuteronomy 31:17–18. For the debate over what this means for prayer, see the note at 7:16.

a: What is my beloved doing in my house
t: A verse the Hebrew and Greek both struggle with
p: The Hebrew is very hard. The Greek reads "vows" for "the many." See the variant.
b: The Hebrew is full of difficulties: "my beloved" (Judah), "her plot with the many," "holy meat," and a last line the grammar does not clearly support. The Greek reads "abomination" and "vows," which makes better sense ("Can vows and holy meat take your evil away?"). The Plain follows the Hebrew and gives the Greek as a variant. Holy meat is the flesh of a sacrifice: the point is again that offerings do not cover sin (7:21–22).

a: A green olive tree, lovely, with fine fruit
p: An olive tree for Israel. Paul's olive tree in Romans 11 is a different picture.
b: Israel is compared to an olive tree in Hosea 14:6 and Psalm 52:8. Here the tree is struck by fire. Paul's olive tree, with branches broken off and others grafted in (Romans 11:17–24), is a new use of the image. The Greek of 11:16 reads "for the voice of its circumcision fire was lit," which differs from the Hebrew "roar."

a: a tame lamb being led away to slaughter
p: Christians have read Jeremiah as a figure of Jesus here. Jewish commentators read it of Jeremiah alone.
b: The word aluf can mean "tame." Rashi (read on Sefaria) reports that Menahem took it as "a large lamb," with support from Targum Jonathan's "choice lamb," while Dunash and Judah ben Kudish read "a lamb and an ox." The Hebrew lechem is "bread, food"; the KJV, ASV, WEB and BSB read "fruit," and Rashi explains the plot to destroy the tree with its bread as a plan to poison his food. The Greek differs (see the two variants): "an innocent lamb" and "put wood into his bread." Early Christian writers read the Greek wording as speaking of Christ. Justin (Dialogue with Trypho 72, about AD 155–160) already quotes the line as Jeremiah's and says Jewish copies had cut it out, and Tertullian (Against Marcion 3.19, about AD 208) reads the wood as the cross laid on Christ's body. The picture of a lamb led to slaughter also recalls Isaiah 53:7, which Acts 8:32 applies to Jesus. Jeremiah himself says only that he did not know the plot.

a: the kidneys
p: The kidneys were the seat of the deepest feelings and conscience.
b: Kelayot, the kidneys, are the hidden inner self, as the heart is the thinking center. God "tests" them (Psalm 7:9; 26:2). In Revelation 2:23 the Greek has "kidneys and hearts." The line of 11:20 repeats in 20:12.

a: the men of Anathoth
p: Anathoth, three miles northeast of Jerusalem, was a priests' village.
b: Anathoth, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem, was the village of Jeremiah's priestly family (1:1). Tradition links the family to Abiathar, the priest Solomon banished there (1 Kings 2:26–27). Why the people of Anathoth wanted him dead is debated: his Temple speech, his criticism of priests, or, as some think, his support for Josiah's reform, which closed country sanctuaries and made them lose income (2 Kings 23:8–9). The text only says they threatened to kill him if he went on prophesying in the LORD's name. His own relatives joined (12:6).

a: You are righteous, LORD
t: Jeremiah's complaint and the question of justice
p: Why do the wicked do well? Job, Psalm 73 and Habakkuk ask the same.
b: Jeremiah argues his case (rib, a lawsuit) with the LORD, reversing the usual direction, in which God sues the people (2:9). He begins by granting that God is in the right. His question, why the way of the wicked succeeds, is that of Job 21, Psalm 73 and Habakkuk 1:2–4, 13. 11:18–12:6 is often counted the first of Jeremiah's "confessions." The answer he gets (12:5) is not an explanation.

a: You are close to their mouths
t: Near in the mouth, far in the heart
p: Isaiah said the same of people who honored God with their lips. Jesus quotes it.
b: People speak God's name but their inner selves are far from him. Isaiah 29:13 says it of lips and heart, and Jesus quotes that verse (Matthew 15:8–9). Jeremiah's word is the kidneys, the deepest self (see 11:20).

a: Set them aside for the day of killing.
t: Consecrate for the day of killing
p: The verb is "make holy." The irony is that sheep are set apart for sacrifice.
b: Haqdishem usually means "make them holy" or "set them apart." Priests set apart an animal for sacrifice. Jeremiah asks that the wicked be set apart the same way, for a day of killing. His own situation, a lamb led to slaughter (11:19), is the opposite.

a: For people have said
p: Rashi hears the wicked saying God will not foresee their end. The Greek has "God will not see our ways."
b: The Hebrew says "he will not see our end." Rashi (read on Sefaria) takes the speakers to be the people who live in the land, saying that what will come of them has not been revealed to him, that is, to God. The Greek says "God will not see our ways." Another way to read the line makes the subject Jeremiah, who will not live to see their end. The Hebrew does not name the subject. See the variant.

a: how can you compete with horses?
t: God answers with a harder question
p: The LORD does not explain why the wicked do well. He asks if Jeremiah can last.
b: The LORD gives no theory of justice. He answers with a challenge: if men on foot have worn you out, how will you keep up with horses? If you feel secure only in a land of peace, what will you do in the thick brush of the Jordan, where lions live? The answer says the harder time is coming, and 12:6 says it will come from Jeremiah's own family. Commentators often note that God does not comfort here but calls Jeremiah to be more, not less, of a prophet. Later Jeremiah's confessions get gentler answers (15:19–21).

a: if you feel secure in a land of peace
p: The Hebrew word means to trust. Some versions read "stumble." The Greek reads "you have not trusted."
b: The Masoretic word boteach is the ordinary verb for "trust, feel secure," and 4QJer-a has the same consonants. The KJV, ASV, WEB and YLT translate it so. The BSB and the NIV read "stumble," and this project's word-by-word line glosses the word "falling." The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition) reads "you have not trusted" (ou pepoithas), which reverses the logic of the verse. The Plain keeps the ordinary meaning of the Hebrew; see the variant for the three readings. "Stumble" would give the argument its edge: if even a safe land trips you, what will the Jordan's thicket do?

a: the Jordan's thick brush
p: The Hebrew is "the pride of the Jordan." It means the thick jungle on its banks, where lions hid.
b: Ge'on hayarden is literally "the pride of the Jordan." It names the dense brush on the river's banks, where lions came to drink (49:19; Zechariah 11:3). The KJV has "the swelling of Jordan," the ASV and WEB "the pride of the Jordan."

a: Your own brothers and the house of your father
p: Jeremiah's kin at Anathoth turn on him, as Jesus' family doubted him.
b: Jeremiah's family were priests of Anathoth (1:1; 11:21). The betrayal is described again in 20:10. In the Gospels Jesus' brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5) and his family thought he had lost his mind (Mark 3:21), and in his hometown a prophet has no honor (Mark 6:4).

a: I have left my house.
p: From here the LORD speaks in the first person, and he grieves.
b: In 12:7–13 the speaker is the LORD, and he talks about "my house, my inheritance, my beloved." Abraham Heschel saw this as the heart of the prophets' message: God is not detached but feels his people's suffering and his own anger (divine pathos). The LORD's leaving his house recalls Ezekiel 10–11, where the glory leaves the Temple.

a: That is why I have come to hate her.
p: To "hate" in Hebrew can mean to reject, as in divorce or covenant language.
b: Sane'ti, "I hate," in covenant language means "I reject." The same word is used of the unloved wife (Deuteronomy 21:15), of Esau in Malachi 1:3 and of the LORD's rejecting his people in Hosea 9:15. It is a statement about the relationship, not an emotion alone, and the promise in 12:15 shows it is not the last word.

a: a speckled bird of prey
p: The Hebrew has a rare word, "speckled." The Greek reads "hyena's cave."
b: The Hebrew ayit tsavua' is "a speckled bird of prey," and the second ayit is the other birds of prey around. The Greek reads "a hyena's cave" for the first (Hebrew tsavua' may be related to the word for hyena). The Plain follows the Hebrew and shows the Greek as a variant. The picture in either reading: the LORD's own land is attacked.

a: They have sown wheat, and they have reaped thorns.
t: Sowing and reaping, the covenant curse
p: Work with no return is a covenant curse. Paul turns it the other way.
b: Deuteronomy 28:38 lists this among the curses: much seed sown, little gathered. Micah 6:15 and Haggai 1:6 describe it, and thorns are the land's curse in Genesis 3:18. Galatians 6:7–8 turns the image to moral life: whatever one sows, one reaps.

a: Be ashamed of your harvests
t: Be ashamed, or they will be ashamed?
p: The Hebrew can be a command ("be ashamed") or a statement ("they will be ashamed").
b: Uvoshu can be read as a command to a group ("and be ashamed") or as "and they will be ashamed," since the same letters serve for both. The next word is "your harvests" (you, plural), which fits a command, and the Greek has a command (aischynthete). The Plain takes the command.

a: I am about to uproot them from their land
t: The neighbors can be restored too
p: The nations that hurt Judah will be uprooted, and then they too may be built up.
b: The verb "uproot" is the one from 1:10, now used on the neighbors. Verses 15–17 then promise that after their uprooting the LORD will have compassion on them too, and if they learn to swear by his name they will be "built up among my people." It is among the earliest places where judgment on the nations ends in an offer. Isaiah 19:24–25 and Zechariah 2:11 go further. If they refuse, the uprooting is final (12:17).

a: I will turn again and show them compassion.
p: Shuv is used of God: he too can turn back.
b: The verb shuv, Jeremiah's word for turning back to God, is here said of God: "I will turn and have compassion." God's turning and the people's turning go together, as in 18:7–10, where the LORD says he may change course if a nation turns.
